people.label: Nick Pope
people.loc: United States (latterly); formerly Main Building, Whitehall, London
people.sub: MoD UFO desk officer, Sec(AS)2a, 1991-1994; author and disclosure commentator
people.narrative: Nick Pope is the single most consequential figure in the British record because he is the only person who ran the Ministry of Defence's UFO desk and then spent thirty years describing what that desk actually did. Born 19 September 1965 to George Pope, an aeronautical engineer at the MoD's Royal Aircraft Establishment at Farnborough, he joined the Ministry of Defence as a civil servant in 1985 and was posted in 1991 to the Secretariat (Air Staff) division that handled unidentified flying object reports, staying three years. Sky HISTORY, the broadcaster for which he worked for over a decade, records that the British programme deliberately had no formal name of the Project Blue Book kind because the government wanted to play down the extent of its own interest. Pope's 1996 book Open Skies, Closed Minds argued from inside knowledge that the MoD's public line - that UFO reports were of no defence significance - did not match the internal handling. When the MoD and The National Archives began releasing the UFO files in 2008 he was approached to help with the publicity and became, in the broadcaster's phrase, the face of the Ministry's new-found transparency, a role that made him the recurring British witness in the 2017-2026 American disclosure wave. In February 2026 he disclosed on social media that he had been diagnosed with stage 4 oesophageal cancer that had metastasised to his liver, writing that he would not have swapped his life 'for the world' and referring to 'the secrets I've been privy to'. His wife Elizabeth Weiss announced that he died at their home on the afternoon of 6 April 2026, aged 60; obituaries followed in The Telegraph, The Times, The Economist and The New York Times through April 2026.
people.tierRationale: Tier A: sole named public holder of the UK's UFO desk portfolio, the official face of the 2008-2013 National Archives release programme, and a primary attesting witness on how a Western government actually handled UAP reporting. Death in April 2026 closes a primary source.

people.label: Dr David Clarke
people.sub: Academic; FOI requester who forced release of Project Condign; National Archives UFO files consultant
people.narrative: David Clarke, a lecturer at Sheffield Hallam University, is the person who actually prised the British record open. In September 2005 he and Gary Anthony, a former British UFO Research Association astronomical consultant, filed a Freedom of Information Act request for the Defence Intelligence Staff study that had been rumoured since the late 1990s. The Ministry of Defence released it on 15 May 2006 as 'Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in the UK Air Defence Region', a four-volume, roughly 400-page study drawing on some 10,000 reports; the MoD's own publication-scheme page records the author as 'DAS' - the Directorate of Air Staff - with the document created and released proactively on 15 May 2006 and an internal review following. Clarke then became the consultant to The National Archives for its UFO file release programme, writing the highlights guide for each of the tranches released between 2008 and June 2013 and fronting the accompanying videocasts and podcasts. His assessment of the material was deliberately unflattering to the MoD's transparency claim: the release did not resolve the phenomenon but did show that the Defence Intelligence Staff had run a far larger investigation than it had ever admitted. The Churchill quotation that The National Archives used to head its UFO pages - 'What does all this stuff about flying saucers amount to? What can it mean? What is the truth?', PREM 11/855, July 1952 - came out of the same body of work.
people.tierRationale: Tier A on disclosure role: his FOI request is the proximate cause of the single most substantive UK government UAP document in the public domain, and he was the archive's own guide to ten tranches of released files.

people.label: Gary Anthony
people.sub: Co-requester of the Project Condign FOI release; former BUFORA astronomical consultant
people.narrative: Gary Anthony, a former astronomical consultant to the British UFO Research Association, filed the September 2005 Freedom of Information Act request jointly with David Clarke that produced the Ministry of Defence's release of the Project Condign report on 15 May 2006. He is the second name on the single most consequential FOI action in the British UAP record. Beyond the request itself the public record on him is thin, which is itself worth noting: the Condign release is routinely credited to Clarke alone in secondary coverage. The request was made under the Freedom of Information Act 2000, which had come fully into force on 1 January 2005 - eight months before the request was filed - so Condign is a direct artefact of the UK statutory access regime rather than of any voluntary MoD decision. The MoD did not release the report immediately; an internal review process is recorded in the Ministry's own disclosure log alongside the release, indicating the request was contested before it succeeded.
people.tierRationale: Tier C: documented as co-requester of the Condign FOI in the report's own release history and in secondary accounts, but with almost no further public footprint.

people.label: Général Denis Letty
people.sub: French Air Force general (2nd Section); founder and chairman of COMETA
people.narrative: Denis Letty, a French Air Force general in the 2nd Section (the reserve of general officers) and an auditor of the Institut des Hautes Études de Défense Nationale, is the man who assembled the most senior group of serving-and-retired defence officials ever to publish a UAP report in a NATO country. In February 1995 he organised a conference on unidentified aerospace phenomena within the Air Force Academy alumni association at which former French military pilots publicly described their own encounters, the CNES officer responsible for the file presented his papers, and an astronomer set out a scientifically acceptable version of the extraterrestrial hypothesis. In March 1995 he took the project to General Bernard Norlain at Norlain's IHEDN office; Norlain referred him to the IHEDN Auditors Association, which backed it. The committee Letty then coordinated over close to three years was named COMETA, the Comité d'Études Approfondies, and was constituted as a French 1901-law association on 24 February 1999 with Letty as chairman. In his own foreword to the report Letty writes that the accumulation of well-documented sightings by credible witnesses 'forces us to consider from now on all of the hypotheses regarding the origin of unidentified flying objects, or UFOs, and the extraterrestrial hypothesis, in particular'. He names his contributors in the text - Jean-Jacques Velasco of SEPRA, pilots Jean-Charles Duboc, Jean-Pierre Fartek and René Giraud, Edmond Campagnac of Air France, Squadron Commander Michel Perrier of the Gendarmerie Nationale, and Air Force General Joseph Domange.
people.tierRationale: Tier A on disclosure role: chaired and signed the only report by senior Western defence figures that recommends diplomatic pressure on the United States over UAP.

people.label: Général Bernard Norlain
people.sub: Former Director, Institut des Hautes Études de Défense Nationale; COMETA preface author
people.narrative: Bernard Norlain is the former director of the Institut des Hautes Études de Défense Nationale, the French state's own senior strategic-studies institute reporting to the Prime Minister, and later a prominent figure in nuclear-disarmament advocacy. His preface to the COMETA report is the reason COMETA cannot be dismissed as a hobbyist product: it places the report inside the IHEDN lineage. Norlain records that Denis Letty came to his IHEDN office in March 1995, that he referred Letty to the IHEDN Auditors Association which supported the project, and that the Association had itself produced a preliminary UFO report in its bulletin some twenty years earlier - the 1976 committee chaired by General Blanchard of the Gendarmerie Nationale whose recommendations produced GEPAN. His preface is titled 'Concrete problems are raised that call for a response in terms of action', and it ends with an explicit political demand: 'I express the wish that the recommendations of COMETA, which are inspired by good sense, will be examined and implemented by the authorities of our country ... May this new report, which is much more in-depth, give new impetus to our national efforts and to indispensable international cooperation. IHEDN will then have well served the nation and, perhaps, humanity.'
people.tierRationale: Tier A on institutional weight: a former director of the French national defence studies institute putting his name to a call for the state to act on UAP is the highest-ranking such endorsement in any NATO country's public record.

people.label: Professeur André Lebeau
people.sub: Former President/Chairman of CNES; COMETA forward author
people.narrative: André Lebeau, a former chairman of the Centre National d'Études Spatiales - the French national space agency, and therefore of the parent body of GEPAN, SEPRA and GEIPAN - wrote the opening forward to the COMETA report under the title 'Stripping the UFO phenomenon of its irrational layer'. Denis Letty states in his own foreword that without Lebeau and Norlain 'COMETA would not have been born'. Lebeau's contribution matters because it is the head of the agency that actually holds France's official UAP case file lending his name to the argument that the subject is a legitimate object of science, and his forward opens by conceding the professional cost: 'It is not looked on highly in certain scientific circles to be preoccupied with phenomena that are deemed to come under the heading of popular mythology', and drawing the analogy to stones falling from the sky - meteorites - which science rejected for centuries before accepting. That analogy is picked up in the report's own conclusion.
people.tierRationale: Tier A on institutional weight: a former head of the French space agency signing the COMETA forward links the private committee directly to the state body that runs the official case database.

people.label: Jean-Jacques Velasco
people.sub: Director of GEPAN 1984-1988 and of SEPRA 1988-2004; COMETA contributor
people.narrative: Jean-Jacques Velasco ran France's official UAP office for twenty years - as director of GEPAN from 1984 to 1988 and then of its successor SEPRA from 1988 to 2004 - which makes him the longest-serving government UAP official in the Western record and the direct counterpart of the American figures on this board. He held the file when the Gendarmerie Nationale was routing sighting reports to CNES by teletype and when CNES could deploy laboratory resources to physical-trace cases, of which the 1981 Trans-en-Provence landing case is the best documented. He was a contributor to COMETA, named in Letty's foreword as 'Jean-Jacques Velasco, Head of SEPRA at CNES', and Wikipedia's account of the report's delivery states that it was Velasco personally who handed the document to Prime Minister Lionel Jospin. He is therefore the hinge between the official French organ and the unofficial general officers' committee: the serving head of the state UAP service participated in a private report that recommended boosting his own service's resources and pressing Washington diplomatically.
people.tierRationale: Tier A: twenty years in charge of the official French UAP service, custodian of the state case archive, and a named contributor to the COMETA report.

people.label: Dr Claude Poher
people.sub: CNES engineer; founding director of GEPAN, 1977-1978
people.narrative: Claude Poher was the CNES engineer who founded and first directed GEPAN, the Groupe d'Étude des Phénomènes Aérospatiaux Non-identifiés, established in 1977 within the French national space agency under the authority of CNES director general Yves Sillard. GEPAN was created on the recommendation of a 1976 committee of the Institut des Hautes Études de Défense Nationale chaired by General Blanchard of the Gendarmerie Nationale, whose objective was 'to make proposals for organizing research and the collection of data on these phenomena' - a fact recorded in the COMETA report's own introduction. Poher's statistical work formed the basis of GEPAN's first year, and a contemporaneous document held in the US National Security Agency's declassified UFO collection records that during 1977 GEPAN 'was largely concerned with checking Poher's statistics, which it approved'. The same NSA-held document records that Poher resigned in 1978 'feeling that he has done everything he could do with the methods at hand', but that the organisation was not disbanded and continued its work.
people.tierRationale: Tier B: founding director of the world's only permanent civilian state UAP office, documented in a US NSA-held contemporaneous assessment as well as in the French record.

people.label: Capitão Uyrangê Bolívar Soares Nogueira de Hollanda Lima
people.sub: Brazilian Air Force captain; commander of Operação Prato, 1977-1978
people.narrative: Captain Uyrangê Bolívar Soares Nogueira de Hollanda Lima commanded Operação Prato, the Brazilian Air Force operation mounted in late 1977 on the island of Colares in Pará after residents reported being injured by descending lights they called the Chupa-Chupa and the mayor, José Ildone Favacho Soeiro, formally asked the Air Force for help. The operation ran in two phases, 20 October to 11 November 1977 and 25 November to 5 December 1977, and was executed by the Brazilian Air Force with the National Information Service, the military dictatorship's intelligence agency. Photographs of lights were taken; the operation was closed after roughly four months and its official finding was that no unusual phenomena had been found. Twenty years later, in 1997, Hollanda gave an interview to the Brazilian ufologists Ademar José Gevaerd and Marco Antônio Petit in which he recounted what he and his men had lived through - an account fundamentally at odds with the official negative finding. Three months after that interview he was found dead at his home, apparently having hanged himself with the belt of his bathrobe. He is the closest thing the Brazilian record has to a custody-adjacent officer who spoke and then died, and the sequence - operation, official denial, twenty years of silence, interview, death - is the reason the case has never settled.
people.tierRationale: Tier A on the combination of command position over a real, documented military UAP operation and a recanting interview followed within three months by his death.

people.label: Brigadeiro Octávio Júlio Moreira Lima
people.sub: Minister of Aeronautics of Brazil; held the 23 May 1986 'Night of the UFOs' press conference
people.narrative: Octávio Júlio Moreira Lima (1926-2011) was Brazil's Minister of Aeronautics on 19 May 1986, the night on which air traffic control at São José dos Campos, the CINDACTA radar network and five scrambled Brazilian Air Force fighters - two F-5Es from Santa Cruz Air Base and three Mirage IIIEs from Anápolis - engaged twenty-one unidentified radar plots over São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Minas Gerais and Goiás. Four days later, at 16:30 on 23 May 1986, he convened a press conference in Brasília and did something no defence minister of a major state had done before or has done since: he produced the intercept pilots and the air traffic controllers in person, confirmed the events, and said on the record that the armed forces had no explanation. His formulation was careful and complete: 'It is not a question of believing or not believing [in extraterrestrials or flying saucers]. We can only give technical information. There are several hypotheses. Technically, I would tell you gentlemen that we have no explanation.' He undertook to investigate and to publish a full dossier within thirty days. The dossier did not appear. The Air Defence Command's own report on the night, dated 2 June 1986 and signed by Brigadier José Pessoa Cavalcanti de Albuquerque, was classified CONFIDENCIAL and not released until 25 September 2009 - twenty-three years later.
people.tierRationale: Tier A on disclosure role: the only serving defence minister of a major air power to hold a press conference with his intercept pilots present and state that the military had no explanation for a mass radar-visual UAP event.

people.label: Brigadeiro do Ar José Pessoa Cavalcanti de Albuquerque
people.sub: Acting Commander, Brazilian Air Defence Command (COMDA/NuCOMDABRA), 1986
people.narrative: José Pessoa Cavalcanti de Albuquerque was the acting commander of Brazil's Air Defence Command when he signed, at Brasília on 2 June 1986, the CONFIDENCIAL Relatório de Ocorrências on the events of the night of 19 May 1986. That document, held in the Brazilian National Archives under reference BR_DFANBSB_ARX_0_0_0249 and released on 25 September 2009, is the most important single sentence in the Latin American record. Its final considerations state that the phenomena produced radar echoes on both the Air Defence System and the interceptors' own airborne radars simultaneously with visual acquisition by the pilots; varied their speeds from subsonic to supersonic and also hovered; varied altitude from below flight level 050 to above flight level 400; sometimes displayed white, green and red lights and sometimes none; could accelerate and decelerate abruptly; and could turn with constant or indefinite radii. Then it concludes, in the command's own voice: 'As a conclusion from the facts constantly observed in almost all the presentations, this Command is of the opinion that the phenomena are solid and reflect in a certain manner intelligence, by the capacity to follow and to maintain distance from observers as well as to fly in formation, not necessarily crewed.' The report also notes, drily, that the Brazilian air defence radar coverage was primarily air-traffic equipment not designed for air defence, which made tracking deficient.
people.tierRationale: Tier A: the signing officer of a primary military document that records an official finding of solid, intelligently behaving unidentified objects - the strongest such statement in any released allied air force record.

people.label: Wilbert Brockhouse Smith
people.sub: Senior Radio Engineer, Canadian Department of Transport; head of Project Magnet 1950-1962
people.narrative: Wilbert Brockhouse Smith (1910 - 27 December 1962) is the earliest named government official anywhere on record to have been told, and to have written down, that the American flying saucer question was classified above the hydrogen bomb and was being run by Vannevar Bush. Smith joined the Canadian Department of Transport in 1939, built Canada's far north ionospheric monitoring system in 1947, and was Canada's chief delegate to the North American Regional Broadcasting Agreement conferences of 1949 and 1950; by 1952 he was Senior Radio Engineer of the DOT's Broadcast and Measurements section, and in 1957 became Superintendent of Radio Regulations Engineering. At the 1950 NARBA conference in Washington he made enquiries of the American scientist Dr Robert Sarbacher and came away with four assertions which he set down in a memorandum, 'Geo-Magnetics', addressed to the Controller of Telecommunications and dated 21 November 1950: that the matter was the most highly classified subject in the United States government, rating higher even than the H-bomb; that flying saucers exist; that their modus operandi was unknown but that a concentrated effort was being made by a small group headed by Doctor Vannevar Bush; and that the entire matter was considered by US authorities to be of tremendous significance. That memorandum was classified Top Secret and was not downgraded to Confidential until 1969. Library and Archives Canada quotes the same memorandum in its own online exhibition: 'the existence of a different technology is borne out by the investigations which are being carried on at the present time in relation to flying saucers ... I feel that the correlation between our basic theory and the available information on saucers checks too closely to be mere coincidence.' The memorandum was the successful request that produced Project Magnet.
people.tierRationale: Tier A: the author of the earliest contemporaneous government document recording that the United States held the saucer question at a classification above the H-bomb under Vannevar Bush, and the author of a 1952 government report recommending acquisition of the technology.

people.sub: Director, CEFAA (Chile), 1997-2016; Director of the Chilean Air Force Technical School
people.narrative: Ricardo Bermúdez Sanhueza, an air brigade general of the Chilean Air Force, became director of the Escuela Técnica Aeronáutica in 1997 and simultaneously took over the direction of the Comité de Estudios de Fenómenos Aéreos Anómalos, the UAP committee that the Director General of Civil Aviation had created on 3 October 1997. The case that made this internationally visible is the Chilean Navy helicopter FLIR video of November 2014, which CEFAA analysed for two years before publishing. Bermúdez's tenure is the model that Canada's own Office of the Chief Science Advisor identified in June 2025 as one of only three worth copying, alongside the American AARO and the French GEIPAN.

people.label: Dr Mona Nemer
people.sub: Chief Science Advisor of Canada; commissioned and signed the Sky Canada Project report
people.narrative: As Chief Science Advisor of Canada, Mona Nemer's office initiated and published the Sky Canada Project, the first Canadian federal review of UAP reporting since the National Research Council stopped collecting reports in 1995. A preliminary report appeared in January 2025 and the full report, 'Management of Public Reporting of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in Canada', in June 2025, running to fifty-nine pages. The report is careful about what it is not - it disclaims any intention to prove or disprove extraterrestrial life or visitors, or to make the Office the point of contact for Canadians reporting sightings - and it is blunt about what it found. Canadians report an estimated 600 to 1,000 UAP sightings a year; a commissioned Earnscliffe Strategies survey found one in four Canadians say they have witnessed a UAP, only ten per cent reported it, and forty per cent would not know whom to contact. Federal departments receive reports but mostly do not compile them, so the government cannot even state how many it receives. The report's recommendations are structural: identify a lead department, establish a dedicated service that collects testimony, investigates and publishes its analyses, get Transport Canada and NAV CANADA to encourage pilots and controllers to report without stigma, open the data, and establish partnerships with AARO and NASA in the United States, GEIPAN in France and SEFAA in Chile. It is the clearest statement by any allied government that the American, French and Chilean models are the ones worth copying.
people.tierRationale: Tier A on disclosure role: her office produced the first G7 government report of the 2020s that recommends building a standing public UAP service and explicitly names foreign partners to join.

people.narrative: Yury Platov of IZMIRAN, the USSR Academy of Sciences Institute of Terrestrial Magnetism and Radio Wave Propagation, was designated chief executive for SETKA-AN at the founding meeting of 18 October 1978 and remained the public scientific face of the Soviet programme. With Vladimir Migulin he published an appeal in the newspaper Nedelya asking members of the public who saw unusual phenomena first to rule out astronomical or familiar objects and then to send descriptions to the Academy's Department of General Physics and Astronomy. With Colonel Boris Sokolov he later co-wrote the 'History of State-directed UFO Research in the USSR', the official retrospective, which sets out the three reasons the programmes were kept secret - their formal status as defence-related activity, the initial assumption of a high probability of military-technical origin, and 'possibilities that in case of successful completion of the raised tasks some of the UFO characteristics could be used for military purposes'. That third reason is the important one: the official Soviet history states in its own words that the programme was concealed partly because its results might be militarily exploitable. Critics of the programme argue that the academic side functioned as a debunking and cover operation for the Ministry of Defence side.

people.label: Dr Ítalo Venturelli
people.sub: Neurosurgeon, Varginha Regional Hospital; Varginha custody witness
people.narrative: Ítalo Venturelli is a neurosurgeon who was on duty at the Regional Hospital in Varginha, Minas Gerais, in January 1996 and who, thirty years later, described to three members of the United States Congress what he says he examined there. On 15 January 2026, in Representative Tim Burchett's office in the Longworth House Office Building, he told Burchett, Anna Paulina Luna and Eric Burlison that a colleague, Dr Marcos Vinico Neves, had sutured a cranial wound on the patient and that he was then asked to examine it visually; he says he was first shown a brief black-and-white video of the patient, then spent three or four minutes at its bedside. His account of what he saw is specific: a body the size of a seven-year-old child, lilac-coloured eyes, teardrop-shaped eyes and cranium, three fingers and a thumb, white skin, a slim torso, no nipples, a small mouth, slivers of ears. He told the members: 'I've been a doctor for forty-six years and have performed thousands of surgeries. To me, it was obvious that this was not a human being.' Asked whether it communicated telepathically he answered: 'I wouldn't say it communicated telepathically; it communicated empathetically, through its eyes.' Neves died in 2018 and, according to Venturelli, no medical records of the procedure were kept. Venturelli says a near-fatal heart attack and other recent medical problems persuaded him in 2025 to break his silence, and that other medical staff could corroborate the account but are afraid because they have been threatened or fear for their careers. He still works full-time at the hospital.

entities.label: Ministry of Defence UFO Desk (Secretariat (Air Staff) / Directorate of Air Staff)
entities.sub: UK civil-service desk receiving and triaging public UAP reports, c.1950s-2009
entities.desc: The 'UFO desk' was the Ministry of Defence's public-facing single point of entry for unidentified aerial phenomena reports from the British public, police, military and civil aviation. It sat within the Secretariat (Air Staff) and latterly the Directorate of Air Staff, and its defining characteristic - attested by its own last desk officer to hold the post publicly, Nick Pope, and by The National Archives' description of the released files - is that it was deliberately never given a project name of the Project Blue Book kind, because the government wished to play down the extent of its interest. The desk's formal public line for five decades was that UAP reports were of no defence significance. The files released by The National Archives between 2008 and 2013 show that the desk simultaneously routed material to the Defence Intelligence Staff section DI55, briefed ministers, answered parliamentary questions, and in the last years handled the largest volume of sighting reports in thirty years. The National Archives' description of the final June 2013 tranche states plainly that it covers 'the final two years of the Ministry of Defence's UFO Desk (from late 2007 until November 2009)' and invites researchers to 'discover the reasons behind the closure of the UFO desk ... and the disclosure campaign for the truth, which was sparked by the closure of the UFO Desk'. The desk was closed on 1 December 2009, the MoD having, in the broadcaster's later summary, 'deemed it surplus to the UK's defence requirements'. The closure took effect nine years after the Defence Intelligence Staff's own Project Condign study had made exactly that recommendation as its single key recommendation.

entities.desc: DI55 was the section of the Directorate of Scientific and Technical Intelligence within the UK Defence Intelligence Staff that quietly held the analytical side of the British UAP question while the MoD's public UFO desk handled correspondence. It is the British counterpart to the American arrangement in which a public project absorbed the reports and an intelligence organisation kept the analysis. DI55 accumulated the roughly 10,000 sighting reports from which the Project Condign study built its database, and Condign's product was issued as a Defence Intelligence Staff Scientific and Technical Memorandum, numbered 55/2/00 - the '55' being DI55's own designator. The report's own recommendation section is a self-liquidation order: its single key recommendation was that 'it should no longer be a requirement for DI55 to monitor UAP reports as they do not demonstrably provide information useful to Defence Intelligence', with a subsidiary recommendation that the database not be maintained. The volume 3 chapter on other countries carries the classification banner UK SECRET UK EYES ONLY and contains a paragraph on the United States and Canada whose operative sentence is a denial - and whose following four lines are redacted.

entities.label: Project Condign
entities.sub: UK Defence Intelligence Staff UAP study, 1997-2000
entities.desc: Project Condign is the codename of the secret study run by the UK Defence Intelligence Staff between 1997 and 2000 whose product, 'Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in the UK Air Defence Region', is the most substantive government UAP analysis released by any American ally. The Ministry of Defence's own description of its origin is precise: 'During a policy review in 1996 into the handling of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena sighting reports received by the Ministry of Defence, a study was undertaken to determine the potential value, if any, of such reports to Defence Intelligence. Consistent with Ministry of Defence policy, the available data was studied principally to ascertain whether there is any evidence of a threat to the UK, and secondly, should the opportunity arise, to identify any potential military technologies of interest.' The second of those two objectives is the one that matters to this board: the British government commissioned a classified study explicitly to see whether UAP could be exploited militarily. Its report, delivered in June 1951, concluded against the reality of the phenomenon and recommended that no further investigation be undertaken - the same shape of conclusion, and the same self-terminating recommendation, that Condign would reach half a century later. The report was itself kept classified for decades and only reached The National Archives in the 2000s. The working party's existence establishes that the British state's engagement with the question is continuous from 1950, predating the MoD UFO desk, and that the recommendation to stop looking has been made and then quietly reversed more than once.

entities.desc: GEPAN was established inside CNES, the French national space agency, in 1977 on the recommendation of a 1976 IHEDN committee chaired by General Blanchard of the Gendarmerie Nationale, with CNES director general Yves Sillard's authority and Claude Poher as inaugural director. It is the first and still the only permanent civilian government UAP office in the world with a published case archive. Its operating model - the Gendarmerie Nationale, the French national police force, teletyping sighting reports directly to the agency, with CNES laboratory resources available for physical-trace analysis - is the single most important institutional difference between the French and Anglo-American approaches. A contemporaneous assessment held in the US National Security Agency's declassified UFO document collection describes GEPAN's June 1978 five-volume, roughly 500-page report to its own scientific council: three special groups (rapid intervention, physical traces, radar alert) had been created; eleven high-credibility, high-strangeness cases were studied in depth, of which only one proved to have a conventional explanation; each case was worked by a four-person team including a psychologist. The NSA-held assessment concludes that 'the care with which distances, angles, and psychological factors were evaluated makes the bulk of the Condon Report seem very poor by comparison', and records that the original French report 'was limited to 120 or 140 copies and was secret'. GEPAN was renamed SEPRA in 1988.

It publishes its own case archive online - it began doing so in March 2007 - with anonymised witness statements and investigation conclusions for each published case. Its four-category classification, rebuilt in 2008, scores each case on consistency (C, the product of quantity and reliability of data) and residual strangeness (E, after testing against known-phenomenon hypotheses): class A, perfectly identified; class B, probably identified; class C, unidentified for lack of data; class D, unidentified after investigation. Its dynamic statistics page dated 11 August 2026 gives 3,381 published cases: 950 class A, 1,310 class B, 1,015 class C, 106 class D. It receives more than 1,000 contacts a year, of which 150 to 200 result in a published investigation. entities.label: Institut des Hautes Études de Défense Nationale (IHEDN)
entities.sub: French national defence studies institute; source of the 1976 committee and the COMETA auditors
entities.desc: IHEDN is the French state's senior strategic-studies institute, whose auditors are drawn from the armed forces, the civil service, industry and the professions. It appears twice in the UAP record, and both appearances are load-bearing. In 1976 a committee of the Institute chaired by General Blanchard of the Gendarmerie Nationale 'opened the unidentified flying objects file' with the objective of making proposals for organising research and data collection on the phenomena; the recommendations of that committee were adopted and produced GEPAN inside CNES in 1977. Twenty years later the IHEDN Auditors Association backed General Denis Letty's new committee, which became COMETA, after Letty took the proposal to the Institute's then director General Bernard Norlain in March 1995. The line of descent means that the French state's official UAP office and the most emphatic senior-officer report on the subject in any NATO country both trace to the same institution.

entities.label: Operação Prato (Operation Saucer)
entities.sub: Brazilian Air Force / SNI field operation, Colares, Pará, 1977-1978
entities.desc: Operação Prato was the first Brazilian Air Force operation mounted solely to investigate UAP. It followed a wave of reports on the island of Colares in Pará in 1977 in which residents said descending lights - which they called the Chupa-Chupa - had burned and punctured them; villagers held night vigils, lit fires and set off fireworks, and the mayor, José Ildone Favacho Soeiro, formally requested Air Force help. The operation was commanded by Captain Uyrangê Hollanda and executed by the Brazilian Air Force together with the National Information Service, the intelligence service of the military dictatorship. It ran in two documented phases, 20 October to 11 November 1977 and 25 November to 5 December 1977, produced photographs of lights, and was terminated after about four months with the official finding that no unusual phenomena had been found. The files are held by the Arquivo Nacional and were opened from the late 1990s onward; Folha de S. Paulo reported in January 2009 under the headline 'SNI investigou óvnis durante a ditadura' that the dictatorship's intelligence service had been running UFO investigations. The operation's importance to this board is that it is a documented case of a military intelligence apparatus mounting a field collection effort against the phenomenon and then publishing a negative finding, with the commanding officer contradicting that finding twenty years later and dying three months afterwards.

claims.text: Operation dates: first phase 20 October - 11 November 1977; second phase 25 November - 5 December 1977; executed by the Brazilian Air Force and the National Information Service; 'Operation found no unusual phenomena'.

entities.label: Noite Oficial dos OVNIs - the Brazilian 'Night of the UFOs', 19 May 1986
entities.sub: 21 radar plots, five FAB fighters scrambled across four Brazilian states
entities.desc: On the night of 19 May 1986 Brazilian air traffic control, the CINDACTA integrated air defence and traffic control network and the Brazilian Air Force engaged twenty-one unidentified radar plots over São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Minas Gerais and Goiás. The sequence, as reconstructed by the Air Defence Command's own report and by BBC Brasil, begins at about 20:00 when air traffic controller Sérgio Mota da Silva at São José dos Campos airport saw stationary multicoloured lights; when he dimmed the runway lights the objects approached, and when he raised them they withdrew. At 21:08 an Embraer Xingu, registration PT-MBZ, flown by Colonel Ozires Silva - the founder of Embraer, returning from a meeting with President José Sarney and due to take office as president of Petrobras the following day - reported large red lights and attempted an unsuccessful approach. Santa Cruz Air Base went to alert at 21:39 and Anápolis shortly afterwards. Five fighters were launched: F-5E FAB-4848 flown by Lieutenant Kleber Caldas Marinho at 22:34 and F-5E FAB-4849 flown by Captain Márcio Brisolla Jordão at 22:50 from Santa Cruz; Mirage IIIEs of the 1st Air Defence Group 'Jaguar' from Anápolis including one flown by Captain Armindo Sousa Viriato de Freitas, plus FAB-4918 (Captain Rodolfo Silva e Souza, 23:17) and FAB-4917 (Captain Júlio Cézar Rozemberg, 23:46). The mission ordered was non-aggressive interception. One F-5 pilot tracked a light that climbed to 33,000 feet while changing from white to red to green, held 10 to 12 miles off, and was followed 180 miles out to sea until bingo fuel. Thirteen radar plots appeared behind the second F-5, which turned 180 degrees and saw nothing. A Mirage closed to two miles of a contact that zigzagged and then accelerated away while the interceptor was already supersonic; in a 1993 TV Globo interview the pilot estimated the object's speed at Mach 15. The objects overflew the National Institute for Space Research and the Aerospace Technical Centre at São José dos Campos and the Air Force Academy at Pirassununga.

entities.sub: CONFIDENCIAL Brazilian Air Defence Command report; declassified 25 September 2009
entities.desc: An eight-page document on Ministério da Aeronáutica letterhead, stamped CONFIDENCIAL on every page, addressed by the Commander of the Air Defence Air Command to the Commander General of the Air, dated Brasília-DF, 2 June 1986, signed by Brigadeiro do Ar José Pessoa Cavalcanti de Albuquerque as acting commander COMDA/NuCOMDABRA, and annexed with a Relatório de Ocorrências. It is scanned and served publicly by the Brazilian National Archives under reference BR_DFANBSB_ARX_0_0_0249 and was declassified on 25 September 2009, twenty-three years after the minister of aeronautics promised a full dossier within thirty days. Its section IV, Considerações Finais, is the operative text: it lists six behavioural characteristics observed and then states the Command's own opinion that the phenomena are solid and reflect a form of intelligence. It also praises the response posture, noting that each engaged air unit maintained an alert aircraft at 45 minutes' readiness and that within under thirty minutes of activation armed vectors were available. It is a document in which a national air defence command tells its own chain of command, in writing and under classification, that it has tracked solid, intelligently behaving unidentified objects that outran supersonic interceptors.

entities.sub: Brazilian National Archives holding of Air Force and SNI UAP records, 1952-2016
entities.desc: From 2009 the Brazilian Air Force transferred its UAP holdings to the Arquivo Nacional, the Brazilian National Archives, where they are served through the SIAN online image system with full archival references and downloadable page images - a materially more open arrangement than the paid-download model The National Archives at Kew used for the equivalent British files. The release began with the September 2009 declassification of the 1986 Air Defence Command report and continued through 2010, when O Estado de S. Paulo reported on 14 August 2010 that the Aeronáutica had released documents on UFO appearances and the news agency EFE reported on 10 August 2010 that the Air Force had created rules for pilots in case of contact with UFOs. The Air Force's own position, given to BBC Brasil, is that all material available on UFOs has already been sent to the Arquivo Nacional and that it 'does not have specialised professionals to carry out scientific investigations or to issue an opinion about this type of aerial phenomenon' - a denial that also functions as a permanent transfer of the question out of the military and into the archive. As of January 2022 the UFO collection was the second most consulted holding in the Arquivo Nacional, behind only the records of the military dictatorship, and spanned sixty-four years, from the 1952 Barra da Tijuca photographs published by O Cruzeiro to a 2016 Brazilian Air Force pilot sighting report.

entities.label: Varginha incident, Minas Gerais, January 1996
entities.sub: Alleged craft crash, capture of nonhuman beings, and alleged US removal
entities.desc: The Varginha case is the only Latin American event that alleges the full sequence this board is built around: a crash, a recovery, custody of biological material, and an American removal. On 13 January 1996, outside Varginha in Minas Gerais, geography teacher and ultralight pilot Carlos de Sousa reported seeing a cylindrical craft trailing smoke come down near a highway; he says he reached the site, smelled ammonia and rotten eggs, picked up a metal fragment that sprang back to shape after he crushed it, and was driven off at gunpoint by soldiers who arrived within minutes. On 20 January 1996 at about 15:20 three young women - Liliane Silva, then 14, her sister Valquíria, 16, and their friend Kátia Xavier, 21 - reported encountering a crouching brown, oily-skinned creature with red eyes, three fingers and a large head in a vacant lot on Rua Dr. Benevenuto Braz Vieira. In 2010 an official Brazilian military inquiry concluded the young women had seen a mentally disabled man nicknamed 'Mudinho', Luiz Antônio de Paula, and that the military vehicle movements were routine maintenance and Fire Brigade activity misinterpreted. Thirty years later the case reached the United States Congress.

claims.text: The 2010 Brazilian military inquiry concluded that 'this citizen, probably being dirty, due to the heavy rains and seen crouching by a wall, was mistaken by the three terrified girls as a space creature', and that the movements of Fire Brigade, Army and EsSA vehicles 'were real facts ... incorrectly interpreted'.

To me, it was obvious that this was not a human being.' He described lilac eyes, a teardrop-shaped cranium, three fingers and a thumb, white skin, no nipples, and 'I wouldn't say it communicated telepathically; it communicated empathetically, through its eyes.'
claims.source: Leslie Kean and Ralph Blumenthal, The Debrief, 30 January 2026

entities.label: Varginha witnesses on Capitol Hill and at the National Press Club, 15 and 20 January 2026
entities.sub: Brazilian witnesses brief three members of Congress on the 30th anniversary
entities.desc: On 15 January 2026, in Representative Tim Burchett's office in the Longworth House Office Building, three members of Congress - Burchett of Tennessee, Anna Paulina Luna of Florida, chairwoman of the House Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, and Eric Burlison of Missouri - held a closed-door session with three Brazilian witnesses to the 1996 Varginha events: neurosurgeon Dr Ítalo Venturelli, forensic pathologist Dr Armando Fortunato, and geography teacher and ultralight pilot Carlos de Sousa. They were brought to the United States by filmmaker James Fox, who with his Brazilian collaborator Marco Aurélio Leal has worked the case for two decades. Jared Moskowitz and André Carson were invited but could not attend. Five days later, on 20 January 2026, Fox convened a public press conference at the National Press Club. Luna said Congress should seek US Air Force flight logs and a landing permit to test the claim of an American retrieval. Retired US Air Force Colonel Fred Claussen set out the documentary trail such a mission would necessarily generate - Air Mobility Command paperwork at Scott AFB, the Air Mobility Wing at Charleston AFB, air-refuelling records and international flight plans - and appealed publicly to the thirty to forty Americans he believes would have direct knowledge. Brazilian Senator Eduardo Girão, who led a Brazilian Senate UAP hearing in 2022, attended in a private capacity and discussed a joint Brazilian-American evidence effort with Burlison. Six further Brazilian witnesses were denied US visas by the State Department on the ground that they might overstay, so their testimony was videotaped in Brazil in December 2025. By 15 July 2026 Representative Burlison had formally asked the FBI and the CIA for records on the case.

entities.label: Project Magnet (Canada)
entities.sub: Canadian Department of Transport UAP and geomagnetic-propulsion study, 1950-1954 (privately to 1962)
entities.desc: Project Magnet was approved by the Canadian Department of Transport on 2 December 1950 following Wilbert Smith's memorandum of 21 November 1950. Its stated goal was to collect data on UFOs and apply anything recovered to practical engineering - specifically to test whether the Earth's magnetic field could be exploited as a propulsion source, which Smith believed the objects were already doing. It drew on Department of Transport facilities with assistance from the Defence Research Board and the National Research Council; Smith's collaborators included Dr James Watt of the DRB, John Thompson of the DOT, Professor J. T. Wilson of the University of Toronto and Dr G. D. Garland of the Dominion Observatory. Its 1952 report is the document that matters: it concluded that the objects were about a hundred feet or more in diameter, capable of several thousand miles per hour and of altitudes above those supporting conventional aircraft or balloons, that 'we are forced to the conclusion that the vehicles are probably extra-terrestrial, in spite of our prejudices to the contrary', and that the next step should be 'a substantial effort towards the acquisition of as much as possible of this technology, which would without doubt be of great value to us'. That is a government engineer, in writing, in 1952, recommending a reverse-engineering programme. In October 1952 Smith set up an instrumented observatory at Shirley's Bay outside Ottawa with a magnetometer, gamma-ray detector, radio receiver, gravity meter and recorders. The Department terminated funding in 1954; Smith continued privately until his death in 1962.

entities.label: Project Second Storey (Canada)
entities.sub: Canadian Defence Research Board committee on flying saucer reports, 1952-1954
entities.desc: Project Second Storey was established in April 1952 by the Defence Research Board, then Canada's military science agency within the Department of National Defence, to examine flying saucer occurrences over Canadian territory as reported by the armed services. It was chaired by the National Research Council astronomer Dr Peter Millman and drew members from Canadian military intelligence and other government agencies, including Wilbert Smith, who reported Project Magnet's findings to it. Its output was procedural rather than investigative: it built a standardised sighting report form and an interrogator's instruction guide with a weighting system intended to minimise the 'personal equation' - an early attempt at scoring witness reliability that anticipates GEIPAN's consistency-and-strangeness scheme by half a century. The form was never broadly adopted. The committee met six times between 1952 and 1954 and concluded that UFOs 'neither posed a security threat, nor were of scientific interest', recommending the end of all investigations by the Canadian military. Its records are held at Library and Archives Canada under RG 24, acc. 83-84/167, box 7523, file DRBS 3800-10-1, pt. 1.

entities.desc: Library and Archives Canada holds the Canadian government's UFO record: files from 1947 to 1995 received primarily from the Department of National Defence, the Department of Transport, the National Research Council and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, with the Department of Communications also represented in LAC's own account. The collection runs to over 15,000 pages, of which around 9,500 have been digitised and are directly available online; the whole collection is publicly accessible and searchable by keywords such as 'UFO' or 'non-meteoritic'. entities.label: Sky Canada Project - Office of the Chief Science Advisor of Canada
entities.sub: Canadian federal review of public UAP reporting, 2022-2025
entities.desc: The Sky Canada Project is the Government of Canada's first formal engagement with UAP since 1995. Led by the Office of the Chief Science Advisor, it published a preliminary report in January 2025 and its full fifty-nine-page report, 'Management of Public Reporting of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in Canada', in June 2025. The project was, in its own words, 'spurred by increased public interest and recent developments in other countries, particularly the United States, where formal procedures for addressing UAP sightings are in development' - which makes it a documented downstream effect of the American disclosure wave on an allied government. Its findings are an indictment of fragmentation rather than of concealment: reports are scattered across federal and non-governmental bodies; most departments do not compile what they receive; the RCMP has no UAP classification at all and logs such calls as non-offence incidents under the Aeronautics Act or as 'suspicious vehicle'; witnesses rarely get a follow-up; and there is no official platform for Canadians to report or to obtain explanations, which the report says 'contributes to the proliferation of misinformation and disinformation'. Its international survey concludes that only the United States, France and Chile provide 'interesting examples of coordinated, transparent, and scientifically driven approaches'. Its recommendations amount to building a Canadian GEIPAN.

entities.label: CEFAA / SEFAA - Chilean anomalous aerial phenomena office, Dirección General de Aeronáutica Civil
entities.sub: Chilean civil aviation UAP office, 1997-present (renamed SEFAA 2021)
entities.desc: The Comité de Estudios de Fenómenos Aéreos Anómalos was created on 3 October 1997 by Gonzalo Miranda Aguirre, the Director of Chile's Dirección General de Aeronáutica Civil, prompted by a sighting wave over Arica in late March and early April 1997 and by the expressed interest of the former Commander-in-Chief of the Chilean Air Force, General del Aire Ramón Vega Hidalgo. Its first director was Colonel Enzo Di Nocera García, with Gustavo Rodríguez Navarro as designated executive secretary; in practice Rodríguez Navarro, an air traffic controller, carried the office in its first years. Ricardo Bermúdez Sanhueza directed it from 1997 to 2016. Rodríguez Navarro and the international relations officer José Lay Lagos left in late 2017. On 18 October 2021, by Resolución Exenta N° 04/3/0113/1385, the body was moved in the DGAC organisation chart to the Subdepartamento Comunicacional and renamed the Sección de Estudios de Fenómenos Aéreos Anómalos, SEFAA. It publishes monthly case-resolution posts - the site carried 'Casos Julio 2026' on 3 August 2026 - and archives resolved cases by year back to 2018. Its stated mission is aviation safety: to support the safety of Chilean air operations through detailed study of each report received, whether from a pilot, cabin crew or a member of the public, with investigations founded on scientific method and heavily dependent on audiovisual records. Its lineage runs back to 1968, when the Chilean Meteorological Office under Colonel Sergio Bravo Flores began collecting reports and forwarding some to the University of Colorado's Condon Committee.

entities.label: Chilean Navy helicopter FLIR case, November 2014 (released January 2017)
entities.sub: CEFAA release of Chilean Navy infrared footage after two years of analysis
entities.desc: In November 2014 a Chilean Navy helicopter on a routine coastal patrol filmed, in daylight and with its infrared camera, an object that the crew tracked from around forty miles away and attempted repeatedly to contact. There was no response. The crew reported it to two nearby radar stations, neither of which could see the object on their screens although both could see the Navy helicopters; air traffic control confirmed that no aircraft had been authorised in the area. The footage shows the object apparently discharging a plume or gas as it moves. CEFAA, then the Chilean civil aviation UAP office, examined the case for two years with a multidisciplinary panel and released the video publicly in January 2017 without an explanation - the first time a Latin American state released military infrared sensor footage of an unresolved object. The release came three years before the US Department of Defense authorised the release of the FLIR1, GIMBAL and GOFAST Navy videos in April 2020, and it establishes the pattern the Canadian government would later identify: the Chilean office publishes what it cannot explain.

entities.label: SETKA-AN / SETKA-MO (later Galaktika, then Gorizont) - Soviet state anomalous phenomena programme
entities.sub: Twin USSR Academy of Sciences and Ministry of Defence programmes, 1978-1990/91
entities.desc: SETKA - 'net' or 'grid' - was the codename for the Soviet Union's twin state programmes on anomalous phenomena, established at the end of 1978 after the sharp increase in reports in 1977-78 and in particular the Petrozavodsk event of 20 September 1977. SETKA-AN ran inside the USSR Academy of Sciences; SETKA-MO ran inside the Ministry of Defence; both were reportedly ordered by the Military-Industrial Commission, which decided to create two research centres that would aid each other and exchange information. A founding meeting took place in the Academy of Sciences on 18 October 1978, attended by Vladimir Migulin and Yury Platov of IZMIRAN (the Institute of Terrestrial Magnetism and Radio Wave Propagation, which became the lead agency), Georgiy Narimanov and Inna Petrovskaya of the Institute for Space Studies, Rem Varlamov of the Moscow Technological Institute, Victor Balashov and Vladimir Volga of secret military unit 67947, A. N. Makarov of the Department of General Physics and Astronomy, Lev Gindilis of the Shternberg State Astronomical Institute, and others including a colonel of the anti-aircraft forces. The programme was renamed Galaktika in 1981 and Gorizont in 1986, and ended around 1990-91, after which a group of experts continued analysing incoming reports in the Department of General Physics and Astronomy of the Russian Academy of Sciences until 1996. Soviet usage substituted 'anomalous phenomenon' for the forbidden term 'UFO'. Guidelines for the Soviet Navy were issued on 7 March 1980 over the signature of the Deputy Commander of the Main Headquarters of the Navy, Vice Admiral Saakyan.

entities.label: Petrozavodsk phenomenon, 20 September 1977
entities.sub: Mass sighting from Copenhagen to Vladivostok; trigger for the Soviet SETKA programmes
entities.desc: On 20 September 1977 a luminous object was reported over an area running from Copenhagen and Helsinki to Vladivostok, and most spectacularly over the Karelian capital of Petrozavodsk, where the TASS correspondent Nikolai Milov described in the mainstream Soviet press - Pravda, Izvestiya, Selskaya Zhizn and Sotsialisticheskaya Industriya - a 'huge star' that flared in the dark sky and spread out 'in the form of a jellyfish, showering the city with a multitude of very fine rays'. Government officials from northern European countries wrote to Anatoly Aleksandrov, president of the USSR Academy of Sciences, asking whether the phenomenon was caused by Soviet weapons testing and whether it threatened the region's environment - which made the event a diplomatic problem as well as a scientific one. A preliminary report to the Academy of Sciences in 1977, assembling visual observations, radiolocation reports, physical measurements and meteorological data, concluded that 'based on the available data, it is unfeasible to satisfactorily understand the observed phenomenon'. By 30 December 1978 Soviet researchers had collected eighty-five reports. The event is the direct trigger for the creation of SETKA-AN and SETKA-MO. It is often attributed to the launch of the satellite Kosmos-955.

entities.label: 'Institute 22' - Soviet Academy of Sciences / Ministry of Defence UFO organisation
entities.sub: Secret Soviet UAP body created 1978, dissolved with the USSR
entities.desc: 'Institute 22' is the name under which the joint Academy of Sciences and Ministry of Defence Soviet UAP effort of 1978-1991 appears in Western secondary literature, chiefly Timothy Good's Need to Know: UFOs, the Military, and Intelligence (2007). On that account it investigated around 3,000 UFO reports and left five to ten per cent unexplained when it dissolved, and orders to observe and report unexplained events were issued widely across the Soviet armed forces without explanation because the Ministry of Defence was involved and no questions could be asked. The label overlaps substantially with what Russian-language sources call SETKA-MO and SETKA-AN, and it should be treated as a Western naming convention for the same apparatus rather than as an independently documented separate body until the primary Russian record is worked. Its principal value on this board is the reporting-volume figure and the confirmation that the Soviet system used routine military tasking to feed a covert analytic centre - the same architecture as the British DI55 arrangement.

claims.text: 'Institute 22' and 'SETKA' most likely denote the same 1978-1991 apparatus under different naming conventions. entities.label: Aerolíneas Argentinas flight AR 674, San Carlos de Bariloche, 31 July 1995
entities.sub: Argentine airliner encounter documented in the May 2026 US Department of War UAP release
entities.desc: On 31 July 1995 Aerolíneas Argentinas flight AR 674, a Boeing 727 under Captain Jorge Polanco, was about 140 kilometres from San Carlos de Bariloche in Patagonia when a power failure blacked out parts of the city and its airport. As the aircraft aligned with the runway an unidentified object showing three lights, including a red one at its centre, appeared off the right side and flew parallel to it; the runway and approach lighting failed again during the manoeuvre. Polanco was unable to land and went around; the object moved behind the aircraft, stopped, ascended vertically, repositioned in front of the aircraft and departed towards the Andes. Another aircraft holding in the area, air traffic controllers and residents on the ground reported the same phenomenon. The case matters here because of where it resurfaced: it appears in the first batch of more than 160 UAP files released by the US Department of Defense on Friday 8 May 2026, in a section of the release examining investigations conducted outside the United States, and the file references a report produced by COMETA - the 1999 French committee. The United States government's own 2026 release therefore cites the French generals' report as a source on a South American case.

entities.sub: Tokyo analyses Pentagon-released files containing sightings near Japan, May 2026
entities.desc: Japan is the clearest 2026 case of an American disclosure action propagating into an allied government. Within days of the first US Department of Defense UAP file release of 8 May 2026, Kyodo News reported on 9 May 2026 that footage disclosed by the United States showed a football-shaped object near Japan; The Japan Times reported on 11 May 2026 that Tokyo was analysing the Pentagon file trove for sightings near Japan; and on 13 May 2026 further coverage reported that the Japanese government had confirmed possession of UAP footage after reviewing the Pentagon videos taken near Japanese airspace, and that Japan would release UAP files of its own. entities.label: United Kingdom Ministry of Defence
entities.sub: UK defence department; owner of the UFO desk, DI55 and Project Condign
entities.desc: The Ministry of Defence is the department that ran the British side of the question from the 1950s to 2009 and that released, under compulsion, the two most substantial British artefacts: the Project Condign report in May 2006 and roughly sixty thousand pages of UFO desk files through The National Archives between May 2008 and June 2013. Its public position throughout was that UAP reports were of no defence significance. Its internal position, as recorded in its own released documents, was that a 1996 policy review commissioned a classified Defence Intelligence Staff study whose second stated objective was 'to identify any potential military technologies of interest'; that the study's chapter on potential related military technology and its paragraph on related military applications were withheld under the defence exemption; and that its chapter on other countries recorded the flat statement that there was 'no intelligence exchange or access or collaboration of any sort' with the United States and Canada on the topic - followed by four redacted lines. The Ministry's Directorate of Air Staff is recorded as the author organisation of the Condign report; its Air Secretariat and Secretariat (Air Staff) held the desk.

entities.label: Release of the Rendlesham Forest files, August 2009 (DEFE 24/1948)
entities.sub: MoD Rendlesham material released in the fourth National Archives tranche
entities.desc: The Rendlesham Forest incident of December 1980 - the events at RAF Woodbridge and RAF Bentwaters in Suffolk, then hosting United States Air Force units, that produced the Halt memorandum and the Halt tape - is the single case that dominates British UAP discussion, and The National Archives' own framing of the August 2009 tranche put it front and centre: the files, covering 1981 to 1996, invited the public to 'find out more about close encounters, stray satellites, bright lights and Britain's very own Roswell - Rendlesham Forest in Suffolk'. That tranche comprised DEFE 24/1948/1, DEFE 24/1959/1 to 1965/1, DEFE 24/1970/1 to 1976/1 and DEFE 24/2086/1. Rendlesham is the point at which the British and American records are physically the same record: the deputy base commander who wrote the memorandum was a United States Air Force officer, the base was a US-operated facility on British soil, and the MoD's own handling of the case sits inside DEFE 24. The case therefore sits directly across the sentence in Project Condign Volume 3 asserting that there is 'no intelligence exchange or access or collaboration of any sort' between the UK and the USA on the topic.

entities.label: The three-office model: GEIPAN, SEFAA, AARO
entities.sub: The only national UAP arrangements a G7 government has endorsed as models
entities.desc: By 2025 exactly three national arrangements had been publicly endorsed by another government as models for handling UAP: the French GEIPAN inside CNES since 1977, the Chilean SEFAA inside the Dirección General de Aeronáutica Civil since 1997, and the American All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office inside the Department of Defense since 2022. The endorsement is in the Canadian Office of the Chief Science Advisor's Sky Canada Project report of June 2025, which surveyed G7 and Commonwealth approaches and concluded that 'the processes in place in a few countries, notably the United States, France and Chile, provide interesting examples of coordinated, transparent, and scientifically driven approaches to UAP reporting'. The common features of the two civilian models are instructive and are the opposite of the British and Canadian histories: a permanent office with a named director, statutory or organisational home in a civil rather than military body, a public intake channel, a published classification scheme, publication of individual case conclusions, and an explicit archive. GEIPAN runs on three full-time staff and more than twenty trained volunteers, with a steering committee chaired by an aerospace expert and including civil and military authorities. SEFAA publishes monthly resolved-case bulletins. Canada's report recommends building the same thing and partnering with all three.

entities.sub: French national space agency; host of GEPAN, SEPRA and GEIPAN since 1977
entities.desc: CNES is the French national space agency and the only space agency in the world that has hosted a permanent UAP office continuously for nearly fifty years. GEPAN was created inside it in 1977 under director general Yves Sillard, on the recommendation of the 1976 IHEDN committee; it became SEPRA in 1988 and GEIPAN in 2005. Norlain's preface to the COMETA report describes the result as 'the only civilian government agency known in the world dedicated to the study of UFOs'. The arrangement gives the office two things no Anglo-American body has had: routine national police reporting into a civil scientific agency, and access to a space agency's laboratory and imaging resources for physical-trace and image-authentication work. CNES also published, in 2007, the book Phénomènes aérospatiaux non identifiés: un défi pour la science under the editorship of Yves Sillard, the former director general who had authorised GEPAN's creation - a former head of the agency returning thirty years later to argue the subject is a challenge for science. In March 2007 GEIPAN opened its archives online.

edges.note: Stonehill and Mantle: the sharp increase in activity in 1977-78, 'especially, the Petrozavodsk Case', forced the Academy of Sciences to agree to the research programme.

edges.note: The 8 May 2026 US release of more than 160 files produced within days an Argentine national story and a Japanese government review.

edges.note: AARO's 2024 report states that no investigation, including foreign efforts, concluded that any UAP report indicated extraterrestrial origin; the Varginha witnesses were briefing Congress against that finding.

edges.note: Published classification, published case conclusions, national police feed, three full-time staff and twenty-plus trained volunteers.

edges.note: SEFAA sits inside the DGAC, publishes monthly resolved-case bulletins and archives cases by year back to 2018.
